chapters.title: Chapter 3: Valuing a Business Against Its Peers

lessons.title: Enterprise Value vs Equity Value: The Bridge Every Manager Should Know

children.text: A promoter agrees to sell his company "for ₹600 crore", tells his family that number, and plans what to do with it. Four months later the money lands and it is ₹412 crore. Nobody cheated him. He agreed a price for the business and received a price for his shares, and those are two different numbers separated by a set of adjustments that were in the term sheet all along.

body.text: Enterprise value is the price of the business. Equity value is the cheque the shareholders receive. Everything between them is somebody else's claim on the company, and every one of those claims is negotiable.

children.text: The Two Numbers
Enterprise value
values the operations. It does not care who funded them.
Equity value
is what is left for shareholders once the lenders and everyone else senior to them are paid.

markDefs.definition: The value of the operating business itself, funded by both lenders and shareholders. It is what a buyer is effectively paying for the operations, before settling who else has a claim.
What belongs to the shareholders after every prior claim is settled. For a listed company this is the market capitalisation.

body.caption: Read right to left for a listed company, left to right in a deal

body.text: Think of buying a flat. The flat is worth ₹1 crore, which is the enterprise value. The seller has a home loan of ₹30 lakh outstanding, which must be repaid out of the sale. The seller walks away with ₹70 lakh, which is the equity value. Nobody argues that the flat is worth ₹70 lakh, and nobody expects the seller to receive ₹1 crore.

children.text: The Bridge, Line by Line

Most Indian deals are agreed on a cash-free, debt-free basis. The buyer names a value for the business and the seller takes the cash out and clears the debt, which in practice happens as a set of deductions from the price.

body.caption: What sits between the two numbers

cells: The buyer must repay it or inherit it
The buyer gets this on day one, so it reduces the real cost
They rank ahead of equity and must be redeemed
A real obligation to employees that arrives with the company
Deduct, or hold back in escrow
The buyer has to fund a decision the seller made
Part of the consolidated business belongs to somebody else
Surplus non-operating assets, such as unused land
Not needed to run the business, so the seller should be paid for them

children.text: Worked Example: Vidarbha Tubes
Vidarbha Tubes Private Limited is a fictional Nagpur steel tubing company with 3 crore shares outstanding. A buyer agrees an enterprise value of ₹600 crore.

body.caption: From ₹600 crore to what the shareholders receive (₹ crore)

cells: Less: bank term loans and working capital limits
Less: redeemable preference shares held by an old investor
Less: working capital shortfall against the agreed normal level

body.title: Vidarbha Tubes: the gap between the headline and the cheque
Build the bridge yourself
body.prompt: A buyer agrees an enterprise value of ₹900 crore for a company with debt of ₹250 crore, cash of ₹60 crore and an unfunded employee liability of ₹40 crore. There is no working capital adjustment. What is the equity value, in ₹ crore?
body.explanation: ₹900 crore - ₹250 crore + ₹60 crore - ₹40 crore = ₹670 crore. If the company has 5 crore shares, that is ₹134 a share. Notice that the employee liability behaved exactly like debt, because that is what it is: money the company owes, payable later.

children.text: The Working Capital Peg, Where Deals Get Tense
A buyer paying for a business expects it to arrive with enough working capital to keep trading. So the parties agree a normal level, and the price is adjusted at closing for any difference.

Vidarbha agreed a normal working capital of ₹50 crore, based on the average of the last 12 months. At closing it was ₹42 crore, because the promoter had collected receivables aggressively and run inventory down in the final quarter. The ₹8 crore shortfall came straight off the price.

body.text: This is why "improving cash flow" before a sale often achieves nothing. Squeeze receivables, stretch suppliers or run down inventory in the last quarter and the working capital peg claws it back rupee for rupee. Worse, diligence notices, and the buyer starts questioning every other number too.

children.text: Indian deals settle this timing question in one of two ways, and the choice decides who owns the cash generated between signing and closing.
Completion accounts.
The price is adjusted after closing, once accounts are drawn up as at the closing date. Accurate, but it invites a fight two months after everyone thought the deal was done.
Locked box.

The price is fixed off an agreed historical balance sheet date. The buyer takes the economics of the business from that date, and the seller promises not to leak value out in the meantime, through dividends, related-party payments or bonuses.
Neither is better in the abstract. What matters is that both sides know which mechanism applies, what counts as leakage, and who prepares the closing statement.
Cash Is Not Always Free, and Debt Is Not Always Labelled Debt
The two easiest lines on the bridge are also where most of the arguing happens.

body.title: What the seller calls it, and what the buyer calls it

columns.label: Seller: "that is all cash"
points: The full closing bank balance, including money needed for next week's salaries
Margin money and fixed deposits pledged against bank guarantees
Cash sitting in a subsidiary that cannot be taken out without tax or regulatory cost
Customer advances received against orders not yet delivered

columns.label: Buyer: "that is not free cash"
points: A minimum operating cash balance must stay in the business
Pledged deposits are restricted, not available
Trapped cash is worth less than cash in the holding company
Customer advances are an obligation to deliver, closer to debt than to cash

children.text: The mirror image applies on the other side. Buyers look for debt-like items that never appear under the heading of borrowings: unpaid statutory dues, overdue creditors stretched well beyond terms, bill discounting, disputed tax demands, deferred consideration owed on a past acquisition, and dividends declared but not yet paid.

body.title: Where did ₹188 crore go?
body.question: The Vidarbha promoter tells his family the company sold for ₹600 crore but receives ₹412 crore. Which statement describes what happened?
options: The buyer reduced its offer during diligence
He agreed a value for the business, and the lenders, preference shareholders, employees and the working capital adjustment were all settled out of that value before the shareholders were paid
The difference is the advisers' fees
Enterprise value is always about 30% higher than equity value
body.explanation: The enterprise value never changed. Every deduction was a prior claim on the same business: ₹180 crore of loans, ₹25 crore of preference shares, ₹15 crore owed to employees, and an ₹8 crore working capital shortfall, less ₹40 crore of cash that came back. Shareholders are paid last here, exactly as in a liquidation, just in happier circumstances.

children.text: The Same Bridge in Listed Markets
For a listed company you start from the other end. The market gives you equity value directly, as market capitalisation, and you add net debt to reach enterprise value.

body.label: Tata Consumer Products and Capital Foods, January 2024
body.context: The acquisition of the owner of Ching's Secret and Smith & Jones was announced at an enterprise value, in a phased purchase. The headline is the value of the business. What the selling shareholders received depended on the target's debt, cash and the adjustments agreed in the share purchase agreement, which is not what the headline reports.

body.text: For companies with more cash than debt, enterprise value is lower than market capitalisation. Large Indian IT services companies usually sit in that position, which is why their EV/EBITDA looks slightly cheaper than their market capitalisation alone would suggest. The cash is already yours the moment you own the shares.

body.title: Reviewing the offer as the seller's CFO
body.scenario: You are CFO of a family-owned auto components business. A private equity fund has offered an enterprise value of ₹750 crore on a cash-free, debt-free basis. Your balance sheet shows term loans of ₹120 crore, working capital limits drawn at ₹85 crore, cash of ₹65 crore including ₹20 crore of fixed deposits pledged against bank guarantees, unfunded gratuity of ₹22 crore, a disputed GST demand of ₹35 crore under appeal, and customer advances of ₹18 crore. The promoter has already told the family the deal is worth ₹750 crore.
body.prompt: What do you prepare before the next negotiation, and what do you tell the promoter?
body.modelAnswer:
What I prepare:
1. A full bridge from ₹750 crore down to expected equity value, with every deduction listed and sourced to a balance sheet line. On the face of it: less ₹205 crore of borrowings, plus ₹45 crore of genuinely free cash, less ₹22 crore of gratuity, which is already about ₹568 crore before the contested items.
2. A position on each disputed item. The ₹20 crore of pledged deposits: argue for release of the guarantees before closing so the cash counts. The GST demand: argue for an escrow or indemnity rather than a full price deduction, since the appeal may succeed. The customer advances: argue they sit inside normal working capital rather than being deducted twice.
3. A working capital peg proposal based on a 12 month average, with the seasonal pattern shown month by month, so the buyer cannot anchor on a low month.
4. A note on what the fund will treat as debt-like that we have not listed: stretched creditors, deferred consideration, declared dividends, related-party loans.

What I tell the promoter:
1. The family will not receive ₹750 crore, and the difference is not a haircut by the buyer. It is the debt and obligations we already owe.
2. Give the family a range, not a number, and give it now rather than after signing.
3. The items worth negotiating hardest are the ones that are genuinely uncertain: the tax dispute, the pledged deposits and the working capital peg. Borrowings are not negotiable, they are arithmetic.
4. Avoid any pre-closing window dressing of receivables or inventory. The peg neutralises it and it costs us credibility we will need for the indemnity discussion.

body.title: The standard basis
body.textWithBlank: Most Indian deals are agreed on a cash-free, ___-free basis, which means the seller keeps the cash and clears the borrowings out of the price.
body.explanation: On this basis the buyer pays for the operating business, and the balance sheet items are settled through the bridge from enterprise value to equity value.

body.title: Before you quote or accept a deal value
steps: Say explicitly whether the number is enterprise value or equity value
List every borrowing, including working capital limits, bill discounting and related-party loans
Split cash into free cash, minimum operating cash and restricted or pledged balances
Identify debt-like items: gratuity, leave encashment, disputed taxes, deferred consideration, stretched creditors
Agree the normal working capital level and the period it is averaged over
Decide the mechanism: locked box from a fixed date, or completion accounts after closing
Confirm the date of the balance sheet all these figures come from
Divide the final equity value by the fully diluted share count, not the current one

body.label: Screener.in: Tata Consumer Products
body.description: Find the market capitalisation on the top panel and the borrowings and cash on the balance sheet tab, then build the enterprise value yourself. Do it for one company in each of three sectors and the bridge will stop feeling abstract.

cards.definition: The value of the operating business, before deciding who has a claim on it.
What shareholders receive after every prior claim is settled.
Borrowings less cash and liquid investments.
The standard deal basis: the seller keeps the cash and clears the debt out of the price.
An obligation that behaves like borrowing even though it is not labelled as such, such as unfunded gratuity.
The agreed normal level of working capital the business must arrive with, with the price adjusted for any difference.
A mechanism fixing the price off an agreed past balance sheet date, with protection against value leakage after it.
Cash that cannot be moved out of a subsidiary or jurisdiction without cost, and is therefore worth less.

points: Enterprise value prices the business. Equity value is what shareholders receive. Always say which one you mean.
Equity value = enterprise value less debt, plus cash, less other prior claims such as preference shares and unfunded employee liabilities.
Vidarbha Tubes agreed ₹600 crore and its shareholders received ₹412 crore, about ₹137.33 a share, with every rupee of difference explainable.
The working capital peg neutralises last-quarter window dressing, so squeezing receivables before a sale usually achieves nothing.
Cash is not always free: minimum operating cash, pledged deposits and trapped subsidiary cash rarely count in full.
Debt is not always labelled debt: gratuity, disputed taxes, stretched creditors and deferred consideration all behave like it.
Deal headlines usually quote enterprise value, as with the ₹5,100 crore enterprise value announced for Capital Foods. The sellers' proceeds were a different number.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment, tax or legal advice. Vidarbha Tubes and the auto components business are fictional, and the treatment of items such as disputed tax demands depends entirely on the wording of the share purchase agreement. The Tata Consumer and Capital Foods figures are from the announcement of that transaction. Take professional advice on any live transaction.
